page.title: How to Choose a Creative Operations Consultant
page.description: A practical checklist for hiring a creative operations consultant: scope, tools, workflows, pricing models and red flags to spot before you sign.
page.h1: How do you choose the right creative operations partner?
page.definition: A creative operations consultant is an external specialist who audits, designs and implements the workflows, tools and governance that let marketing and creative teams move from brief to publish with fewer revision rounds and predictable cycle times.
page.quick_answer: Start with a paid assessment that maps your current intake, review and publishing steps, then ask the consultant to deliver a prioritised use-case list, a tool recommendation and a 90-day roadmap with owners and metrics.

sections.h2: What should the first engagement deliver?

blocks.p: The consultant should produce an assessment, a prioritised use-case list, a tool choice and a roadmap. That output lets you decide whether to continue with the same partner or hand the plan to an agency for build-out.

ul: Current-state map of intake, brief, production, review, approval, publishing and reporting
Bottleneck ranking with cycle-time data or stakeholder interviews
Shortlist of work-management, review and asset-management tools matched to team size
90-day roadmap with owners, milestones and core metrics: cycle time, revision rounds, on-time rate, capacity use

sections.h2: Consultant versus agency: which do you need?

blocks.p: Consultants deliver strategy and tool selection; agencies deliver working automations, integrations and documentation, often with a support retainer. Choose based on whether you need a plan or a built system.

head: Factor
Consultant
Agency
rows: Assessment, use-case list, tool choice, roadmap
Fixed build fee plus monthly retainer
Three to six months plus retainer
Daily stand-ups, sprint reviews, QA sign-off

sections.h2: Which tools should appear in the recommendation?

blocks.p: A credible recommendation names specific categories and explains why each fits your volume, approval layers and existing stack. Avoid generic lists that could apply to any team.

ul: Work management: Adobe Workfront, Asana, Monday.com or Wrike

sections.h2: What does a realistic creative ops team structure look like?

blocks.p: Five roles cover the full lifecycle; small teams combine them in one producer. The consultant should map each role to a named person or a clear outsourcing plan.

head: Role
Primary responsibility
rows: Round tracking, stakeholder chasing, version control
CMS push, QA checks, metadata, scheduling
Cycle-time dashboards, revision trends, capacity forecasts

sections.h2: What are the red flags during the sales conversation?

blocks.p: Beautiful decks without concrete workflow diagrams, tool-agnostic claims that hide a preferred vendor relationship, and promises to "fix everything" without a phased roadmap signal a partner who will bill hours rather than deliver change.

ul: No request for current cycle-time data or revision-round counts before quoting
Single-tool recommendation without a comparison table
No named owner for each roadmap milestone
Pricing only as a retainer with no fixed assessment phase
Case studies that show only creative output, not operational metrics

sections.h2: How do you structure the first 90 days after hiring?

blocks.p: A first plan runs 90 days: long enough to see a trend, short enough to change course. Break it into three monthly sprints with clear gates.

ol: Month one: run the assessment, agree tool shortlist, pilot intake form on one campaign
Month two: implement work-management template, set up review workflow in Frame.io or Figma, measure baseline cycle time
Month three: roll out asset library structure, automate hand-offs with Zapier or Make, deliver dashboard with cycle time, revision rounds, on-time rate, capacity use

faq.q: How much does a creative operations assessment cost?
faq.a: West Peek Productions scopes creative operations work per engagement and does not publish a fixed price. Send the scope for a quote.

faq.q: Can the same partner run the assessment and build the system?
faq.a: Yes, but separate the contracts. Keep the assessment fixed-price and short, then decide whether to extend into a build retainer based on the roadmap quality.

faq.q: What metrics prove the engagement worked?
faq.a: Track cycle time from approved brief to publish, average revision rounds per asset, on-time delivery rate and team capacity utilisation. Improvements should appear within the 90-day window.

faq.q: Should we keep strategy and brand voice in-house?
faq.a: Keep in-house: strategy, brand voice approval and product decisions. Outsource moderation, member support, programming, onboarding and reporting to free internal bandwidth.

faq.q: How do we avoid tool lock-in after the consultant leaves?
faq.a: Require the roadmap to include export paths, API documentation and a runbook for each integration. The consultant should hand over a living Notion or Confluence space, not just a slide deck.
